title: Invert Binary Tree
description: Swap each node’s left and right children recursively — the mirror image of the original tree.

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down the inputs.
sections.say:
"So I need to invert a binary tree — by 'invert' you mean produce the mirror image, where every node's left and right children are swapped, and that swap cascades through all descendants. Yes? (As opposed to, say, reversing the values per level or rotating the tree.)"

Then a few quick clarifying questions:
• Mutate in place, or return a new tree?
• Node shape — `{ val, left, right }` with `null` for missing children?
• What should I return for an empty tree — `null`?
• Are duplicate values allowed? (Doesn't change the algorithm but worth confirming.)
sections.why: The 'mirror' framing is the clearest plain-English description and pins down what's actually being asked. In-place vs. new-tree matters for the API: the canonical answer mutates and returns the same root, which is fine for LeetCode but a real codebase might want immutability. The empty-tree question surfaces the base case before you write it. This is the famous Max Howell tweet problem — Google rejected him for failing it on a whiteboard, so the bar for crisp execution is high.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.say:
"There isn't a meaningfully slower 'brute force' here — the natural recursive solution is already O(n) and visits each node once. I'd describe it as: at every node, swap the left and right children, then recurse into both subtrees so they get inverted too. Base case: null returns null. Three or four lines.

The only variation worth mentioning is whether you swap first then recurse, or recurse first then swap — both work, the order of operations doesn't affect correctness because the recursive calls are independent."
sections.why: Calling out that there's no slower variant — and that the order doesn't matter — is the move. Interviewers worry about candidates who pad with a strawman; saying 'the natural solution is already optimal, here's why the order doesn't matter' shows you've thought about it rather than memorized it. The order-independence callout is a frequent interviewer follow-up; pre-empting it saves a round-trip.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern
sections.prompt: What signal in the problem points to pure tree recursion?
sections.say: "Mirror is a per-node transformation defined recursively: the mirror of a tree rooted at N is a tree with N's value, the mirror of N.right as left subtree, the mirror of N.left as right subtree. Each node's output depends only on its two children's outputs — that's the textbook signature of structural recursion on a tree. So I'd do exactly that: base case null returns null, recursively invert both children, swap. This is also the classic 'exam of recursion' problem — the algorithm is so trivial that what's being tested is whether you can write clean recursive code under pressure, not algorithm design. So I'd focus on writing it cleanly first and only optimize if asked."
sections.why: The 'exam of recursion' framing is the key insight. The interviewer almost certainly isn't testing whether you know the algorithm — they're testing whether you can express it in clean code without thinking. Calling that out tells them you understand what's actually being graded, which is itself a signal of interview maturity.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few inputs to confirm the model before writing the loop.
sections.intro: "Let me trace through a couple of cases to make sure my model is right." Three inputs cover the interesting behaviors — a balanced BST whose inversion has a clean property (inorder becomes sorted descending), the empty tree, and a tiny asymmetric tree that shows the structural change.

examples.note: Classic balanced BST — inversion produces the mirror; inorder traversal goes from sorted ASC to sorted DESC.
examples.trace:
invert(4)
  invert(2)
    invert(1) → leaf, swap nulls, return 1
    invert(3) → leaf, swap nulls, return 3
    swap 2's children: now left=3, right=1; return 2
  invert(7)
    invert(6) → leaf, return 6
    invert(9) → leaf, return 9
    swap 7's children: now left=9, right=6; return 7
  swap 4's children: now left=7, right=2; return 4
final: root=4, left=7 (with children 9,6), right=2 (with children 3,1)

examples.note: Degenerate — base case returns null immediately, no recursion.
Tiny asymmetric — shows the swap turning a left-only child into a right-only child.
examples.trace:
invert(1)
  invert(2) → leaf, return 2
  invert(null) → return null
  swap 1's children: now left=null, right=2; return 1

sections.why: The BST trace is the cleanest sanity check: inverting a BST should make its inorder traversal go from sorted-ascending to sorted-descending. If your code is wrong, that property will visibly break. The `[1,2]` trace exposes the subtle bug where a careless implementation forgets to assign the swapped result — if you only recurse into existing children, the lone child never moves to the other side.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases to mention
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Before I declare it done, let me think about edges:
• Null root → base case returns null. ✓
• Single node → no children to swap, returns unchanged.
• Perfectly balanced tree → all swaps happen, recursion depth is log₂(n).
• Left-skewed (degenerate to linked list) → becomes right-skewed. Recursion depth equals n, so a million-node skewed tree would overflow the call stack. The iterative alternative uses a queue or stack — same swap logic, no recursion.
• All-same values → swap is structurally identical to the original tree; inorder traversal is unchanged, but the references on left/right have flipped. Worth mentioning that visual equivalence doesn't mean object identity.
• Asymmetric subtrees (e.g. lots of lefts, few rights) → recursion handles it naturally because each subtree is processed independently."
sections.why: The skewed-tree callout is the senior signal — for a degenerate tree the recursion depth equals n, which is the same O(h) space concern that shows up across every tree problem. The all-same-values observation about reference vs. value equality is the kind of subtle thing that separates engineers who think about object identity from those who only think about output. Either prompt earns you bonus points.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity claim?
sections.say:
"Time is O(n) — every node is visited exactly once. Work per node is constant: two recursive calls and a swap.

Space is O(h) for the recursion stack, where h is the tree height. Balanced is O(log n); skewed is O(n) worst case. If the interviewer pushes back on stack safety, I'd convert to iterative BFS or DFS — push root onto a queue/stack, pop, swap children, push the children back, repeat. Same O(n) time, O(w) extra space where w is max level width (or stack size).

If you wanted to extend this to 'check if a tree is a mirror of itself' — Symmetric Tree, LeetCode 101 — you'd use parallel recursion on the original tree against its mirror, comparing values and inverted subtrees at each step. Same recursive shape, different combine step. And of course the Max Howell rejection is the canonical interview folklore here — if you can't write this in 60 seconds under pressure, you'll get filtered. The drill is to make it muscle memory."
sections.why: The iterative fallback is the right answer to the stack-overflow pushback. The Symmetric Tree extension demonstrates you see invert-tree as a primitive in a family of mirror problems, not just a one-off question. Surfacing the Howell folklore is appropriate here in a way it wouldn't be for most problems — it tells the interviewer you know this problem's reputation, which signals you've taken it seriously enough to make the implementation reflexive.

walkthrough.intro: Step through the recursive invert on a real tree. The trace simulates post-order recursion with an explicit stack — each node's children are inverted before its own swap. The final return is flattened back to level-order for comparison.
trace: if (!arr || arr.length === 0 || arr[0] == null) return null;
const root = { val: arr[0], left: null, right: null };
if (i < arr.length && arr[i] != null) { node.left = { val: arr[i], left: null, right: null }; q.push(node.left); }
if (i < arr.length && arr[i] != null) { node.right = { val: arr[i], left: null, right: null }; q.push(node.right); }
yield { line: 1, label: `enter invertTree — tree ${JSON.stringify(input)}`, state: { treeShape: input } };
yield { line: 2, label: 'root is null → return null', state: { treeShape: input, returns: JSON.stringify([]) } };
yield { line: 2, label: `root=${root.val} not null`, state: { treeShape: input, root: root.val } };
yield { line: 3, label: `call invertTree(${node.val}) — descend left then right`, state: { treeShape: input, current: node.val, stackDepth: stack.length } };

yield { line: 5, label: `at node ${node.val}: swap children — left=${r ? r.val : 'null'}, right=${l ? l.val : 'null'}`, state: { treeShape: input, current: node.val, newLeft: r ? r.val : null, newRight: l ? l.val : null, stackDepth: stack.length } };
yield { line: 7, label: `return inverted tree → ${JSON.stringify(out)}`, state: { treeShape: input, inverted: out, returns: JSON.stringify(out) } };

notes: Pure recursive swap — recurse first, then assign, so children are independently inverted before the swap.
Base case `if (!root) return null` covers empty trees and terminates at leaf children.
O(n) time, O(h) space; h = O(log n) balanced, O(n) skewed.

alternates.label: Iterative BFS queue
alternates.when: Reach for this when the tree could be adversarially skewed — deep enough to blow the JS call stack (~10k+ levels). Any traversal order works for invert because each swap is independent, so BFS is the cleanest iterative shape.
notes: Push root, pop, swap children, push the (now swapped) children — order of push doesn't matter because each swap is local.
Space is O(w) — the queue holds at most one level; on a balanced tree that is ~n/2 at the bottom, heavier than recursion's O(log n) average but bounded by width not call-stack depth.
A DFS stack version is identical — just replace queue.shift() with stack.pop(). Both are O(n) time, only the traversal order and space constant differ.

questions.q: What does invertTree do at every node?
options: Replaces the node's value with its sibling's value
Swaps the left and right children
Sorts the children by value
Negates the node's value (val → -val) and recurses
root is a leaf — return root immediately without recursing
root is null — return null
root.left and root.right both null — return a fresh node with the same val
Recursion depth equals tree height — return root to unwind
O(log n)
O(n) — each node visited once
O(n log n)

questions.q: Space complexity of the recursive version (call stack)?
options: O(h) where h is the tree height
Always O(log n)

questions.q: Can you invert a tree iteratively, and if so with what data structure?
options: No — invert requires recursion
Yes — a BFS queue OR a DFS stack both work; pop a node, swap its children, push the children back
Only a priority queue works
Only a hash map works
questions.explain: The swap is independent per node, so any traversal order works — a queue (BFS) or a stack (DFS) both correctly visit every node to swap.

questions.q: Pre-order and post-order both work for invert, but plain in-order is awkward. Why?
options: In-order visits each node twice (once between left and right, once on return), so swaps happen twice and cancel out
After you swap a node's children, an in-order traversal's 'left then right' no longer refers to the original sides, so you can double-swap or visit wrong subtrees
In-order requires the tree to be a BST; the inverted tree's in-order ordering breaks the BST invariant mid-traversal
In-order is iterative-only in JS, so it can't perform the swap during recursion
questions.explain: Swapping mid-traversal changes which child in-order visits next; pre/post-order swap before or after both recursions, avoiding the confusion.

questions.q: Does the order — swap-then-recurse vs recurse-then-swap — affect correctness?
options: Yes, only recurse-then-swap is correct
Yes, only swap-then-recurse is correct
No — the two recursive calls are independent of the swap, so either order produces the same mirrored tree
It depends on whether the tree is a BST
questions.explain: Each subtree is inverted independently of the swap at the current node, so the operations commute.

questions.q: What is the base case that makes the recursion terminate?
options: When root is a leaf — return root without making the two recursive calls
When root is null — return null (or just return), so leaves' null children stop the descent
When root.left === root.right — both are null, so the swap is a no-op and we return early
When the recursion stack reaches the tree's height — unwinding terminates the descent
questions.explain: Hitting null is the floor of the recursion; without it you'd dereference null.left and crash.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the recursive swap; inorder traversal of the inverted BST should be sorted DESC.

blanks.hint: new right = inverted ORIGINAL left (saved in tmp)

L3.prompt: Write `invertTree(root)` that swaps every node’s children in place. Log the inorder traversal of the inverted BST [4, 2, 7, 1, 3, 6, 9]. Expected reversed order.
hints: Recurse left and right first, THEN assign the swapped results.
Inorder of a BST is sorted ASC; after inversion it becomes sorted DESC.
